output.name: Lamet
output.myth: When old Tenu went aloft, his grandchildren sewed his name onto a strip of sailcloth, one knot for each letter. They flew it at midsummer, when the light stays late. Ennu the Kite-Wright built the frame, and Aun showed him how to bend it without asking first. The name-kite climbs the Lamp Road with its tail behind, so every star that sees it knows who is passing. Tavo came over the north ridge to tear the strip, because Tavo laughs at names and cannot be bargained with. Tavo had laughed at the Hat the Gale Kept, far off in the north-west, and was in no mood to be gentle. Hulun the Crook lies south-west, where Hesk turns names uphill the way herders turn goats. Hesk, at the pole, did not look up. She keeps count. She marks each name as it passes her string and lets none go. The strip is knotted to the bright star at the tail, where the name stays when the cloth wears thin. So we tie our names on. The wind does not read. Hesk does.
output.finding: Find Hulun, the Herder's Crook, then look one fist (about 11°) to its north-east, where the name-kite hangs on the Lamp Road with its tail behind it.
